
90 Vanadians

Merry and blessed Christmas to everyone!
It is finally Christmas (and remains so for the next 12 days). I love to tell the Christmas Story as it is given to us in St. Luke’s Gospel. I would like to include fireworks, but haven’t figured out how to pay for them or how to avoid running afoul of management and the fire marshal. I know this story so well for reasons of love, I don’t really need to read or study it any more. Even so, something was bugging me this year and that is an unmistakable sign that I need to spend some more time with Bible in hand, reading the text several times.

Of course there was all the usual stuff I recognize, and reminders of things our long held traditions have gotten wrong. Perhaps my favorite of the things we've gotten wrong over the years is that Jesus was not born in manger, he was *placed* in a manger. A manger is a feed trough and not some kind of barn. He was placed in the manger because there was no space in the *guestroom*. That word usually translated as *inn* is more properly rendered *guestroom*. It also makes far more overall sense to read, "Jesus was placed in the food trough because there was no space in the guest room." These are the sorts of things that keep theologians up at night (that and four-alarm chili).

Anyway, I could go, but I couldn't shake the feeling there was some detail just ever so slightly out of my reach. I started to ask myself, "Why did St. Luke, and only St. Luke, choose to tell us the story of the shepherds in the field? After all, he couldn't tell us everything, so why this? It is a lovely story, but the writers of Scripture don't include details just because they are interesting or lovely. The Gospel writers wrote with purpose. In this case I couldn't figure out what the purpose was. I was stuck with an enjoyable story.

More reading is better than less when it comes to understanding Scripture. Here is what I should have known, but had to re-discover: The Angel Gabriel comes to the Blessed Virgin Mary and says of Jesus, "He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High. And the Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end" (Luke 1:32-33). And in case you missed it, Gabriel tells Mary her yet to be born baby will be a king and a king forever. This was the AH-HA moment.

When a king is born, who do you tell about the birth? Reason dictates that - short of the mother and father - other royalty should be the first to know. And the announcement should be accompanied by great fanfare - perhaps even fireworks (OH! How I would love to have fireworks for Christmas!).

So: Who knows about the birth of Jesus and in what order? Obviously Mary was the first to know, her and whatever other women were attending her. Then follows Joseph who is likely outside wringing his hands along with some of the other men of Bethlehem who were likely trying to comfort Joseph with wine.

Who of great nobility and eminence is next in line to hear of the royal birth? This is actually a trick question as I have already alluded to the answer and I confess I have led you astray. You might be tempted to say The Three Kings - even King Herod had to rely on them to get the news. The Three Kings would be a good guess, but it would be wrong.

The next to hear about the royal birth of Jesus are the shepherds in the field.

At this point, I suppose we should recognize that God thinks about things differently than we do. Pomp, grandeur, solemnity, and office do not seem to impress Him. If they did, I don't think shepherds keeping their sheep in the fields would be on the A-list.

"An angel of the Lord appeared to them and the glory of the Lord shone around them, and they were filled with great fear."

Small wonder they were filled with great fear, here they were, minding their own business, probably telling stories and passing the wine around - as shepherds are want to do. I am not sure it helped all that much when the angel said, "Fear not."

The angel goes on to say, "I bring you good news of great joy that will be for all the people." Admittedly, it's subtle, but the angel is inferring the shepherds are the first to know. The angel continues with, "for unto you is born this day in the city of David a Savior who is Christ the Lord." The shepherds will know this to be the case because they are given a sign, a new born baby in Bethlehem.

As if this were not enough, the poor shepherds, scared out of their wits, now find themselves surrounded by a heavenly host "praising God and saying, 'Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among those with whom he is pleased.'"

One does not normally set out to be a shepherd. It is not a glamorous job. Sheep, as cute as they may be, what they lack in intelligence they more than make up for with questionable aroma. And yet, as big a deal as the birth of Jesus is in heaven, it is the shepherds who are honored by the heavenly host.

One last unusual thing that should hold our attention: The 23rd Psalm informs us that the Lord is our shepherd. It is of great significance that Our Father in Heaven chooses to be a shepherd - the caretaker of the not so bright and aromatically challenged - that would be us. He is the Shepherd of the shepherds. It should come as no surprise that the great heavenly announcement comes first to the people of Our Father's profession.

What Christmas message can we take from all this? First, and obviously, God does not think like we do. That doesn't sound very Christmas-y. Perhaps more Christmas-y is the answer to the question, *who does God come for?* He does not come first for the bright and shiny, but for those in need. There you go, the true meaning of Christmas - Jesus comes and embraces those who need him most.
